'''''Pachycereus pringlei''''' (also known as '''Mexican giant cardon''' or '''elephant cactus''') is a species of large [[cactus]] native to northwestern [[Mexico]], in the states of [[Baja California]], [[Baja California Sur]], and [[Sonora]]. It is commonly known as '''''cardón''''', a name derived from the Spanish word ''cardo'', meaning "thistle"; additionally, it is often referred to as '''sabueso''' (or "bloodhound"), which is possibly an early [[Spanish colonialist]] interpretation of the [[Seri people|Seri]] word for the plant, '''xaasj'''.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.loscabosrestaurantguide.com/cardon_cactus.htm |title=Cardón cactus, ''Pachycereus pringlei'' |first=Bob |last=Chamlee |publisher=Los Cabos Guide to Good Eating and More! |access-date=2011-11-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060415085445/http://www.loscabosrestaurantguide.com/cardon_cactus.htm |archive-date=2006-04-15 }}</ref>

Large stands of this cactus still exist, but many have been destroyed as land has been cleared for cultivation in Sonora.

Climate change will likely affect the future distribution of numerous plant species, including ''Pachycereus pringlei,'' which can be attributed to alterations in precipitation and temperature.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Urban |first=Mark C. |date=May 2015 |title=Accelerating extinction risk from climate change |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aaa4984 |journal=Science |language=en |volume=348 |issue=6234 |pages=571–573 |doi=10.1126/science.aaa4984 |pmid=25931559 |bibcode=2015Sci...348..571U |issn=0036-8075|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

The [[Cactus#Food|cactus fruit]]s were always an important food for the Seri people, in Sonora; the dried cactus columns themselves could be used for construction purposes, as well as for firewood.<ref name="Felger1985">*{{cite book |last=Felger |first=Richard |author2=Mary B. Moser. |title=People of the desert and sea: ethnobotany of the Seri Indians |location=Tucson |year=1985 |publisher=University of Arizona Press |isbn=0-8165-0818-6 |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/peopleofdesertse0000felg }}</ref>

The cactus thrives in barren landscapes thanks to a remarkable symbiotic relationship with a [[Biofilm|biofilm]] that forms on its roots. This biofilm enables the cactus to colonize bare rock, even in the absence of soil. This makes this species an opportunistic [[lithophyte]]. The root's bacterial colonies can [[nitrogen fixation|fix nitrogen]] from the air and break down the rock to expose hidden sources of nutrients. The cactus has evolved to maintain cultures of the symbiotic bacteria within its dormant seeds.<ref name="Ref_">{{cite journal |first=M. E. |last=Puente |author2=Y. Bashan |author3=C. Y. ==Morphology==
A cardon specimen is the tallest{{Ref|1}} living cactus in the world, with a maximum recorded height of {{convert|19.2|m|ftin|abbr=on}},<ref name="Salak">{{cite journal |first=M. |last=Salak |title=In search of the tallest cactus |journal=Cactus and Succulent Journal |volume=72 |issue=3 | pages= 163–164}}</ref><ref name="TallestSaguaro"/> with a stout trunk up to {{convert|1|m|ftin|abbr=on}} in diameter bearing several erect branches. In overall appearance, it resembles the related [[saguaro]] (''Carnegiea gigantea''), but differs in being more heavily branched and having branching nearer the base of the stem, fewer ribs on the stems, blossoms located lower along the stem, differences in [[areole]]s and spination, and spinier fruit.

The [[flower]]s are white, large, nocturnal opening, and appear along the ribs as opposed to only [[Shoot apical meristems|apices]] of the stems.

==Lifespan and growth==
An average mature cardon may reach a height of {{convert|10|m|sigfig=1}}, but individuals as tall as {{convert|18|m|sigfig=1}} are known.<ref>(León de la Luz and Valiente 1994).</ref> It is a slow-growing plant<ref>(Roberts, 1989)</ref> with a lifespan measured in hundreds of years. One way scientists have aged these cacti has been to use radiocarbon dating to test the spines closest to the ground.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Delgado-Fernández |first1=Mariana |last2=Garcillán |first2=Pedro P |last3=Ezcurra |first3=Exequiel |date=September 2016 |title=On the Age and Growth Rate of Giant Cacti: Radiocarbon Dating of the Spines of Cardon ( Pachycereus Pringlei ) |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/S0033822216000254/type/journal_article |journal=Radiocarbon |language=en |volume=58 |issue=3 |pages=479–490 |doi=10.1017/RDC.2016.25 |bibcode=2016Radcb..58..479D |s2cid=130664993 |issn=0033-8222 |via=Cambridge Journals|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Growth can be significantly enhanced by  inoculation with the bacteria ''[[Azospirillum]]''.<ref>(Bashan et al., 1999</ref><ref>Carrillo et al., 2000</ref><ref>Puente and Bashan, 1993</ref> Most adult cardon have several side branches that may be as massive as the trunk. The resulting tree may attain a weight of 25 tons.<ref>(Gibson and Nobel, 1986).</ref>

''Pachycereus pringlei'' has [[psychedelic drug|psychedelic]] effects and appears to have been used by ancient people in [[Baja California]], [[Mexico]], as an [[entheogen]] and for various other uses.<ref name="Azarius2005">{{cite web | title = 'Brand new' psychedelic discovered | date = 11 January 2005 | url = http://www.azarius.net/news.php?newsindex=89 | quote = Hit of the Sacred Elixir Conference (San Jose, California on October 22–24) was Earl Crockett's presentation on "a new elixir" in which Earl described his adventures in Baja California discovering a pictoglyph-covered cave and an alleged cactus that was ingested by the inhabitants (who predated the Indians--Earl speculates by thousands of years). He shared the stage with Alexander Shulgin who told of how he analyzes new chemical compounds and how Earl's cactus - Pachycereus pringlei - was indeed a brand new kind of psychedelic. Cactouasca: Sasha outlined the four basic types of one-compound psychedelics and then described ayahuasca which is a two-compound psychedelic--1) a DMT analogue plus 2) an MAO inhibitor to prevent the first from being destroyed. There are many varieties of ayahuasca that differ in the plant substances that provide these two components--that is, many different plants that carry DMT and many plants that carry MAO inhibitors. There is even something called "pharmauasca" which is not derived from plants at all but which is simply synthetic DMT (in a capsule) and synthetic MAO-inhibitor in another capsule. Earl's cactus was different from all of these--it contained a lot of MAO inhibitor but no DMT. (DMT, says, Shulgin is found everywhere in nature but never in cactuses). Instead in Earl's cactuses there were mescaline-like substances that have no psychoactive effects on humans--by themselves. Shulgin's guess is that the presence of the MAO-inhibitor in the cactus protects the mescaline-like molecule from degradation and hence permits it to act on the brain in a mescalin-like way. So Earl's cactus is indeed a "brand new elixir"--a heretofore unexplored two-compound psychedelic for which Shulgin coined the term "cactouasca". Some of Heffter's selfexperiments revealed nothing of interest and, specifically, no effects remotely resembling those of mescaline. [...] A variety of simple isoquinoline alkaloids were later examined vs. monoamine oxidases (MAOs) [58]. The only cactus alkaloids included were carnegine (both enantiomers), racemic O-methylanhalonidine and Omethylpellotine, and some members of the newly discovered (since 1985) 5,6,7,8-tetraoxygenated Pachycereus alkaloids. R-(+)- carnegine proved to be a rather potent competitive MAO-A inhibitor, with a 2 μM Ki value, while its enantiomer was fifty times less potent. O-Methylanhalonidine and O-methylpellotine were weaker than S-(-)carnegine, with Ki values of 160-170 μM, and the 5,6,7,8-tetraoxygenated analogs were several times less potent. None of these showed significant inhibition of MAO-B. [...] The fairly potent MAO-A inhibitory action of carnegine suggests that this and similar alkaloids, if present in a cactus or one of its extracts, might potentiate the effects of mescaline.}}</ref> According to Shulgin, ''N''-methylmescaline, in [[combination drug|combination]] with MAOIs also present in the cactus that allow ''N''-methylmescaline to become [[oral administration|orally active]], may be the active psychedelic constituent.<ref name="Trout2013a" /><ref name="Trout2013b">{{cite book | author = [[Keeper Trout & friends]] | title = Trout's Notes on The Cactus Alkaloids Nomenclature, Physical properties, Pharmacology & Occurrences (Sacred Cacti Fourth Edition, Part C: Cactus Chemistry: Section 1) | date = 2013 | publisher = Mydriatic Productions/Better Days Publishing | pages = 149–150, 159, 161, 163, 170, 174, 187, 204 | url = https://troutsnotes.com/pdf/C13_CactusAlkaloids.pdf | quote = N-Methylmescaline: Human studies show no effects at levels of 25 mg. Some of the alkaloids in ''Pachycereus pringlei'', like carnegine, are known to be [[Neurotoxicity|neurotoxic]] in [[Animal testing|laboratory animals]].<ref name="Trout2013b" /><ref name="Cassels2019" />

==Notes==
:1.{{Note|1}}The tallest living cactus is a specimen of ''Pachycereus pringlei''. The tallest cactus ever measured was an armless [[Saguaro]] cactus which blew over in a windstorm in 1986; it was 23.8 meters (78 feet) tall.<ref name="TallestSaguaro">{{cite news|title=Windstorm Fells 78-Foot Cactus--Tallest in World |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1986-08-01-mn-19025-story.html |access-date=2015-08-04 }}</ref>
